text: SAS enables a great deal of flexibility by 47 allowing user programming to specify components, effects, and data distribution for regression with non-linear mixed models. To fit the mixed models, the SAS procedure maximizes an approximation to the likelihood integrated over the random effects. SAS uses adaptive Gaussian quadrature and a first-order Taylor series approximation for the approximation to the likelihood and a large variety of algorithms for the maximization. During the modeling process, SAS outputs the final maximized value of the log likelihood (-2 log likelihood,) as well as the Akaike information criterion (AIC), its small sample bias corrected version (AICC), and the Bayesian information criterion (BIC). Different models for the same datasets can be compared by comparing the AIC, AICC, and BIC scores. Smaller scores indicate better fitted models. During the modeling process, variables with a p-value larger than 0.5 were excluded from the models. For variables with a p-value between 0.05 and 0.5, the model fitness measures were used to determine if they should be included in the models. 4.1.3.2 Linear Mixed Models Similar to the negative binomial regression with random effects, linear mixed models (LMMs) are an extension of traditional linear models to allow both fixed and random effects. Most variables in these models are binary variables, and LMMs were simply utilized to compare differences of the observed data for the analysis scenarios. 4.1.3.3 Generalized Linear Model and T-Test For the crime data analysis, the project team used both t-tests and generalized linear model (GLM) regression using the SAS® software package. SAS uses the TTEST procedure to perform t-tests for one sample, two samples, or paired observations (SAS Institute, 2013b). For mean comparisons, the t-test is particularly suitable for analysis when the two samples are independent, and the data are normally or lognormally distributed in each sample.
